messages.content:
You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Stone

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'stone' (and the closely related 'rock') most commonly symbolizes Jesus Christ himself, especially as the rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone/foundation of God's building (the church), and simultaneously as a stone of stumbling for unbelievers. The New Testament writers explicitly apply the Old Testament 'stone' texts christologically, and this reading has been dominant from the patristic era onward.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Psalm 118:22 (the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone)",
    "Isaiah 28:16 (a tested, precious cornerstone laid in Zion)",
    "Isaiah 8:14 (a stone of stumbling, a rock of offense)",
    "Daniel 2:34-35, 44-45 (the stone cut without hands that destroys the statue and becomes a great mountain, read christologically/messianically)",
    "Matthew 21:42-44 and parallels (Mark 12:10-11; Luke 20:17-18)",
    "Acts 4:11 (Peter applies Psalm 118:22 to Jesus)",
    "Romans 9:32-33 (stumbling stone in Zion applied to Christ)",
    "Ephesians 2:20 (Christ Jesus himself the cornerstone)",
    "1 Peter 2:4-8 (the living stone, cornerstone, and stone of stumbling all applied to Christ)",
    "1 Corinthians 10:4 (the rock that followed Israel was Christ)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Believers as 'living stones' built into a spiritual house/temple upon Christ the cornerstone \\u2014 the church as God's building.",
      "basis": [
        "1 Peter 2:5",
        "Ephesians 2:19-22",
        "1 Corinthians 3:9-17"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "God himself as 'the Rock' \\u2014 a title of stability, refuge, and faithfulness (often merged with the christological reading but originally a divine epithet).",
      "basis": [
        "Deuteronomy 32:4, 15, 18",
        "Psalm 18:2, 31",
        "Psalm 62:2, 6-7",
        "2 Samuel 22:2-3"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Peter as the rock on which the church is built \\u2014 dominant in Roman Catholic interpretation; Protestant traditions often read the rock as Peter's confession or as Christ, making this a materially contested reading.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 16:18"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Stones as memorials or witnesses \\u2014 standing stones, altars, and cairns commemorating covenant events (Bethel, Gilgal, Ebenezer).",
      "basis": [
        "Genesis 28:18-22",
        "Joshua 4:1-9, 20-24",
        "Joshua 24:26-27",
        "1 Samuel 7:12"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Stone as hardness/deadness of the human heart, contrasted with a heart of flesh in regeneration.",
      "basis": [
        "Ezekiel 11:19",
        "Ezekiel 36:26",
        "2 Corinthians 3:3",
        "Zechariah 7:12"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Stone tablets of the Law \\u2014 stone representing the old covenant written externally, contrasted with the Spirit writing on hearts.",
      "basis": [
        "Exodus 31:18",
        "2 Corinthians 3:3, 7"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The 'white stone' with a new name given to the overcomer \\u2014 variously read as acquittal, admission (tessera), or personal acceptance by Christ; no agreed interpretation.",
      "basis": [
        "Revelation 2:17"
      ],
      "prominence": "unclear"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The Daniel 2 stone read specifically as the kingdom of God (rather than Christ personally) crushing worldly empires \\u2014 emphasized in some eschatological traditions (e.g., historicist and Latter-day Saint readings).",
      "basis": [
        "Daniel 2:34-35, 44-45"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "Consensus is strong because the New Testament itself performs the interpretation: Jesus, Peter, and Paul all quote the Old Testament stone texts (Psalm 118:22; Isaiah 8:14; 28:16) and apply them directly to Christ, and 1 Peter 2:4-8 gathers all three into a single christological catena. The main genuine interpretive divergence concerns Matthew 16:18 (Peter vs. Peter's confession vs. Christ), which is a confessional dividing line rather than a challenge to the broader Christ-as-cornerstone consensus. Secondary meanings (living stones, memorial stones, stony hearts, tablets of law) are widely acknowledged but treated as distinct sub-motifs rather than rivals to the primary meaning."
}

      ],
      "prominence": "common"

  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "The primary Christological consensus centers on Christ as both the foundation of the Church and the rock of offense. Context dictates secondary symbols, most notably spiritual stubbornness in the Old Testament prophets and believers as living stones in the New Testament epistles."
}

RESPONSE C
{
  "primary_meaning": "Christ as the rejected yet chosen cornerstone—the secure foundation of salvation, faith, and the people of God.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Psalm 118:22: the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone.",
    "Isaiah 28:16: God lays in Zion a tested, precious cornerstone as a sure foundation.",
    "Matthew 21:42; Mark 12:10–11; Luke 20:17: Jesus applies the rejected-stone text to himself.",
    "Acts 4:11–12: Jesus is the rejected stone who became the cornerstone, with salvation found in him.",
    "Romans 9:32–33: Christ is both the stone over which unbelievers stumble and the one in whom believers trust.",
    "1 Peter 2:4–8: Christ is the living, chosen cornerstone; he is also a stone of stumbling to the disobedient.",
    "Ephesians 2:20–22: Christ is the cornerstone of the spiritual temple formed by God's people."
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "God or Christ as rock-like strength, protection, permanence, and refuge.",
      "basis": [
        "Deuteronomy 32:4",
        "Psalm 18:2,31,46",
        "Psalm 62:2,6–7",
        "1 Corinthians 10:4"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Believers collectively as “living stones” built into the Church or spiritual temple.",
      "basis": [
        "1 Peter 2:5",
        "Ephesians 2:21–22"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Spiritual hardness, insensibility, or resistance to God, especially in the expression “heart of stone.”",
      "basis": [
        "Ezekiel 11:19",
        "Ezekiel 36:26",
        "Zechariah 7:12"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "An obstacle of stumbling, offense, judgment, or ruin for those who reject God or Christ.",
      "basis": [
        "Isaiah 8:14",
        "Daniel 2:34–35,44–45",
        "Matthew 21:44",
        "Romans 9:32–33",
        "1 Peter 2:7–8"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The divinely established kingdom that destroys worldly kingdoms and fills the earth, represented by Daniel's stone; some Christian traditions identify the stone more directly with Christ.",
      "basis": [
        "Daniel 2:34–35,44–45"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "A memorial, witness, or enduring testimony to God's acts and covenant commitments.",
      "basis": [
        "Genesis 28:18–22",
        "Joshua 4:1–9,20–24",
        "Joshua 24:26–27",
        "1 Samuel 7:12"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The permanence and authority of divine law, associated with commandments written on stone tablets.",
      "basis": [
        "Exodus 31:18",
        "Exodus 32:15–16",
        "2 Corinthians 3:3,7"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "A new identity, acquittal, victory, or admission to the messianic banquet, symbolized by the white stone in Revelation; the exact background is disputed.",
      "basis": [
        "Revelation 2:17"
      ],
      "prominence": "unclear"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "“Stone” is highly context-dependent and has no single settled symbolic meaning across Scripture. The dominant specifically Christian use is christological—Jesus as the rejected stone and cornerstone—but hardness, refuge, stumbling, the Church, memorial testimony, and God's kingdom are also established readings."
}

  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "In Christian biblical interpretation the dominant and most frequently taught symbolic use of 'stone' is christological (cornerstone/rejected stone/living stone), drawing especially on the NT's explicit application of OT stone texts to Jesus. Related but distinct uses (God as Rock, believers as living stones, Daniel's kingdom-stone) are also standard and widely recognized; they do not displace the primary christological consensus. Purely negative or non-messianic readings are secondary."
}

BOOK ENTRY
A person as a building member of a house or kingdom. Jesus is the rejected living Stone made the chief cornerstone; His people are living stones built under and aligned to Him. The Stone cut without hands is Christ as Head of the kingdom that grows into the Mountain filling the earth.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
(none)

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Isa 28:16; Ps 118:22; Dan 2:34-35, 44-45; Matt 21:42; Eph 2:20-22; 1 Pet 2:4-7) · see Mountain, ch. 39

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
